# Hutsix â€” Windows Automation Toolkit

Hutsix is a Windows automation toolkit with keyboard macros, OCR and image screen triggers, and trained AI image triggers. Free 7-day trial, then a one-time $49 USD license, for Windows 10/11.

## What Hutsix does

- Keyboard Macros â€” Map and fire keyboard actions from global hotkeys.
- OCR & Image Triggers â€” Detect on-screen text and visual patterns you define.
- Trained AI Triggers â€” Train a detection model on your own screenshots and use it as a trigger; template matching with a calibrator covers simpler cases.
- Profiles â€” Switchable profiles with foreground-window detection.

Free 7-day trial with the full feature set, no card required. After it ends, a license is a one-time $49 USD with no subscription; the trial cannot be reset by reinstalling.

## How it works

Hutsix organizes automation into profiles made of bindings. Each binding pairs a trigger with an action: a trigger detects an event (global hotkey, mouse input, pixel color, image match, OCR text, or a trained AI image model), and an action plays a keyboard or mouse sequence. When a profile is active, a watchdog engine continuously evaluates bindings and executes actions only when the configured conditions are satisfied.

1. Install a Hutsix release and launch the app.
2. Create or import a profile.
3. Add a trigger (hotkey, mouse, pixel color, image match, OCR text, or AI image).
4. Attach an action sequence (keyboard or mouse playback).
5. Activate the profile and validate behavior with the Action Monitor and per-binding diagnostics.

## Use cases

- Gaming: Auto-looting in MMOs, buff management and ability rotations, frame-perfect input sequences for fighting games.
- Productivity: Data-entry automation from screenshots, form filling with OCR detection, batch processing triggers.
- Accessibility: Map a long key sequence to a single key, or run a routine that is hard to repeat by hand.
- Developer Tools: UI testing automation and screenshot-based regression testing workflows.

## System requirements

- OS: Windows 10 or Windows 11, 64-bit
- Administrator rights: required to install
- Internet: required for first license activation, with an offline grace period afterwards
- Hotkeys, macros, pixel and template triggers: 2 CPU cores (4 recommended), 8 GB RAM, no GPU
- OCR text and AI image triggers: 4+ CPU cores, 16 GB RAM recommended; CUDA GPU with 4-8 GB VRAM optional, and without one they check about twice a second
- Training your own detection model: 16-32 GB RAM, CUDA GPU with 8 GB+ VRAM, 10 GB+ free space for datasets
- Storage: the installer downloads about 3.4 GB; plan on 10 GB free
- Display: multi-monitor and HDR displays supported

Hutsix runs both CPU and GPU execution paths. CUDA acceleration applies to supported AI and vision workloads, and every feature falls back to the CPU when a GPU is unavailable.

## Privacy

Hutsix is a local desktop application. Profiles, logs, and runtime data are stored locally on your system. Licensing checks may contact the licensing provider during activation or verification.

## FAQ

Q: Is Hutsix free?
A: Hutsix has a free 7-day trial with the full feature set. After it ends, a license is a one-time $49 USD - there is no subscription.

Q: Does Hutsix work with Windows 11?
A: Yes â€” Hutsix supports Windows 10 and Windows 11, 64-bit.

Q: Can the Hutsix trial be reset by reinstalling?
A: No. The trial is anchored on your machine and cannot be reset by reinstalling the app.

Q: Is coding required to use Hutsix?
A: No. Typical usage is fully UI-driven; no custom scripts are needed.

Q: Can I share my profiles?
A: Yes. Profiles are reusable and shareable through import and export.

Q: Does Hutsix inject into game memory?
A: No. Hutsix is designed around input simulation and screen/foreground detection.

Q: Does Hutsix support GPU acceleration?
A: Yes. CUDA-enabled acceleration is available for supported AI and vision workloads, with automatic CPU fallback when a GPU is unavailable.

Q: Can automation violate third-party terms?
A: Yes. Some apps and services prohibit automation. Users are responsible for how they use the software.
